title: The Indus: the river that made Pakistan
description: From the glaciers of Tibet to the Arabian Sea, the Indus built one of the world's first civilisations, gave its name to a subcontinent, and still feeds Pakistan today. A Maps and Musings documentary.

lines: It begins as a trickle of meltwater, high on the Tibetan Plateau, more than five thousand metres above the sea.
From there, it travels more than three thousand kilometres, through some of the highest mountains on Earth, and across the plains, to the Arabian Sea.
Along the way, it built one of the world's first great civilisations, gave its name to a whole subcontinent, and today it feeds a nation of more than two hundred and forty million people.
This is the story of the Indus.

shots.chapter_name: From the roof of the world
shots.text: From the roof of the world

lines: The Indus rises in western Tibet, near the sacred Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar. Tibetans call it the Senge Tsangpo, the Lion River.
It flows north-west through Ladakh, in Indian-administered Kashmir, and then into Gilgit-Baltistan, in Pakistan.
On the way, it gathers rivers fed by the great glaciers of the Karakoram and the Himalaya.
Near Skardu, the river winds past the cold desert of Katpana, where sand dunes lie beneath snow-capped peaks.
Further west, the river carves its way through deep, narrow gorges.
Here, the Indus passes beneath Nanga Parbat. At eight thousand one hundred and twenty-six metres, it is the ninth-highest mountain in the world.
Then the river turns south, and begins its long journey down towards the plains.
It leaves the mountains at Tarbela, and flows past Attock, where it is joined by the Kabul River from Afghanistan.
In Punjab, five great rivers, the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, gather together, and join the Indus near Mithankot.
That is where Punjab gets its name: the land of five waters.
Then the Indus crosses Sindh, the province that takes its name from the river, and reaches the Arabian Sea, south of Thatta.
Around four and a half thousand years ago, the banks of the Indus were home to one of the world's first great civilisations.

clips.label: Dholavira
clips.sub: An Indus civilisation city, Gujarat, India

lines: Its two largest cities were Harappa, on the Ravi, and Mohenjo-daro, beside the Indus in Sindh. Both are in today's Pakistan.
Mohenjo-daro may have been home to around forty thousand people, in a carefully planned city of brick houses, streets and drains.

events.text: Mohenjo-daro becomes a UNESCO World Heritage Site

lines: The civilisation stretched from Balochistan to near today's Delhi. It traded with Mesopotamia, and it had its own script, which no one has yet been able to read.
Harappa was identified in nineteen twenty-one, and Mohenjo-daro in nineteen twenty-two. In nineteen eighty, Mohenjo-daro became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

shots.small: Sanskrit for 'river': the root of Sindh, Indus and India
lines: The river also gave its name to far more than a civilisation. Its ancient Sanskrit name, Sindhu, gave us Sindh, and through Persian and Greek, the words Indus and India.
In the nineteenth century, the British began building modern canals to carry the river's water to farmland.
Today, the Indus and its tributaries feed what the World Bank calls the largest connected surface-water irrigation system in the world, with thousands of kilometres of canals.
A chain of barrages along the river, from Chashma and Taunsa in Punjab to Guddu, Sukkur and Kotri in Sindh, turns the river into these canals.
Much of Pakistan's wheat, rice, cotton and sugarcane depends on this water.
In the north, the river is held back by Tarbela Dam, completed in nineteen seventy-six.
It is one of the largest earth and rock filled dams in the world, and its lake stretches for about eighty kilometres.
Tarbela stores water for the dry season, and generates hydroelectric power.
When British India was partitioned in nineteen forty-seven, the new border cut straight across the Indus river system.
The rivers rise in India or flow through it, but Pakistan's farms depend on them downstream.
In nineteen sixty, after nine years of talks facilitated by the World Bank, the two countries signed the Indus Waters Treaty.
Pakistan received the western rivers: the Indus, the Jhelum and the Chenab. India received the eastern rivers: the Ravi, the Beas and the Sutlej.
The treaty survived wars and crises for more than sixty years.

events.text: Court of Arbitration: treaty 'remains fully in force'

lines: But in April twenty twenty-five, after an attack on tourists in Indian-administered Kashmir that killed twenty-six people, India announced it was placing the treaty in abeyance.
India says this will last until Pakistan ends what it calls support for cross-border terrorism. Pakistan denies any involvement in the attack.
On the thirty-first of August twenty twenty-six, the Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled unanimously that the treaty remains fully in force, and that India cannot suspend it on its own.
India did not take part in the case. It rejected the ruling, calling the court illegally constituted.

shots.text: Every single drop of Pakistan's water is our red line.
lines: Pakistan's prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, has said that every single drop of Pakistan's water is a red line.
For now, the treaty's future remains uncertain, and with it, the water on which millions of people depend.
The Indus is also home to one of the rarest mammals on Earth: the Indus river dolphin, known locally as the bhulan.
It is almost blind, and finds its way and its food in the muddy water using sound.
It lives only in the Indus river system, and is listed as endangered. Its range has shrunk by around eighty percent, largely because barrages have cut the river into sections.

shots.caption: Indus river dolphins counted in 2017 (WWF-Pakistan survey)
lines: A WWF-Pakistan survey in twenty seventeen counted one thousand eight hundred and sixteen dolphins, most of them between the Guddu and Sukkur barrages in Sindh.
The good news is that their numbers have grown since the early two thousands, thanks to conservation efforts.
At the end of its journey, the Indus spreads out into a vast delta, south of Thatta.
But very little of the river now reaches the sea. Dams, barrages and canals take most of its water long before it gets here.
Water researcher Hassan Abbas says the delta once received around one hundred and eighty to two hundred million acre-feet of water a year.
Under a nineteen ninety-one agreement, it should now get at least ten million. But in twelve of the past twenty-five years, it did not.

shots.caption: Area of the Indus delta (km²)
lines: A twenty nineteen study by the US-Pakistan Center for Advanced Studies in Water found that the delta shrank from about thirteen thousand nine hundred square kilometres in eighteen thirty-three, to about one thousand and sixty-seven in twenty eighteen.

shots.small: of the Indus delta lost since 1833
lines: That is a loss of ninety-two percent.
As the river retreats, the sea moves in. In Kharo Chan, only three of its forty-two villages remain. The rest have been swallowed by the sea.
Its population fell from twenty-six thousand in nineteen eighty-eight, to about eleven thousand in twenty twenty-three.
From the glaciers of Tibet to the mangroves of Sindh, the Indus has shaped this land for thousands of years.
It fed some of humanity's first cities. It feeds Pakistan today. And its future will shape the lives of millions more.
This was the story of the Indus. Thank you for watching Maps and Musings.
